I will keep my land in the crop pattern I know best: winter wheat followed by summer maize. In Quzhou, that is still the steadiest way for me to make grain, use my machinery well, and avoid taking on too much market and management risk. I am 65, so I do not want a crop that needs too much hand labor or too many complicated field decisions. Cotton can make sense in some places here, but for me it is slower to manage, more laborious, and the cash return is less certain than grain. Wheat and maize fit our local weather, our irrigation habit, and the way our county farms now.

I will put most of my effort into keeping inputs moderate and timely rather than chasing the very highest yield. Wheat needs the water more in our area, so I will save irrigation for wheat’s key stages and keep maize mostly on summer rain with only one emergency watering if needed. I will use improved seed, not the cheapest traditional seed, because I want reliable emergence, lodging resistance, and stable yield. I will also keep fertilizer balanced instead of pushing nitrogen too hard, because our area has already learned that too much fertilizer wastes money and does not always add yield. My plan is to keep the whole year simple, mechanized, and steady.
